title: APR Calculator: how it works, formula and examples

content:
The [APR Calculator](/apr-calculator) is a free online tool on CalcHub. Estimate a loan's annual percentage rate after upfront fees, not just its advertised interest rate. Enter your loan amount, advertised annual interest rate, upfront finance fees and loan term and the result appears straight away — no account or download needed. Because it runs entirely in your browser, the values you type never leave your device, and you can use it as often as you like.

Annual percentage rate (APR) expresses the yearly cost of borrowing, including eligible upfront finance charges as well as interest. Two loans can advertise the same note rate but have different APRs when one charges higher origination fees. This calculator finds the rate that matches the fixed payments to the money you actually receive after fees, making competing personal, auto and home-secured loan offers easier to compare. This guide explains how to use it, the formula it applies, and a worked example you can follow with your own numbers.

## How to use the APR Calculator

Start by entering your loan amount, then entering your advertised annual interest rate (%), entering your upfront finance fees and finally entering your loan term (years). The result updates as you type, so adjust any value and watch the answer change. If the answer is not what you expected, check the value you entered first — a missing digit or a wrong unit is the usual cause.

1. Enter the full amount financed and the lender's advertised annual note rate.
2. Add prepaid origination, application or other required finance fees, then enter the repayment term.
3. Compare the estimated APR and total borrowing cost between offers with the same amount and term.

## Formula

Payment = P·r ÷ (1 − (1+r)⁻ⁿ). APR is found by solving net proceeds = payment × (1 − (1+a)⁻ⁿ) ÷ a for monthly APR rate a, then multiplying a by 12 × 100.

That is the standard formula for this calculation, and it is the same one the [APR Calculator](/apr-calculator) applies to the values you enter. You can work it out by hand, but the calculator is faster when you want to try several values, and it removes the risk of a slip in the arithmetic.

## Worked example

Here is a typical example. A 20,000 loan at 7.5% for five years has a payment of about 400.76. If 750 of required fees leaves 19,250 in net proceeds, the estimated APR is about 9.12%, rather than 7.5%. Try the same figures in the [APR Calculator](/apr-calculator) and you will get the same result — then change one value at a time to see how the answer moves.

## What the result shows

With the default values (Loan amount: 20000, Advertised annual interest rate: 7.5 %, Upfront finance fees: 750, Loan term: 5 years), the [APR Calculator](/apr-calculator) returns Estimated APR: 9.12%, Monthly payment: 400.76, Net amount received: 19,250, Interest plus upfront fees: 4,795.54, Effective annual rate: 9.52%. The first figure is the headline result, and the rest break it down so you can see how the total is made up. If you want to compare with a related calculation, the [Loan Calculator](/loan-calculator) is worth a look before you finish.

## Why APR can be higher than the note rate

The note rate determines the contractual payment on the amount financed. Fees reduce the useful proceeds without reducing that payment, so the return required on the net advance is higher. APR spreads those upfront charges across the expected life of the loan. With a very short term, the same fee produces a much larger APR difference because there are fewer payments over which to spread it.

## What this estimate does not include

APR rules and included charges vary by country and loan product. Optional insurance, late charges, early-settlement penalties and costs that would apply even in a cash purchase are not automatically included. For a regulated quotation, use the APR disclosed by the lender and check whether repayments, compounding and fees match the assumptions used here.

## Tips

A few things worth knowing before you rely on the result — most of them are about the numbers you put in, rather than the tool itself:

- Compare offers over identical terms; extending a term can hide fees behind a lower payment.
- Separate optional add-ons from mandatory finance charges before entering fees.
- Use total interest plus fees as a second comparison, especially if you expect to repay early.

## Frequently asked questions

### Is APR the same as the effective annual rate?

No. Nominal APR annualises the monthly percentage-rate calculation without compounding it. The effective annual rate also shows the effect of monthly compounding and is normally slightly higher. Try it with your own numbers in the [APR Calculator](/apr-calculator) — the result updates as you type, so you can test a few scenarios in seconds.

### Why is my lender's APR different?

The lender may include a different set of regulated charges, use daily rather than monthly timing, or account for an irregular first payment. Their regulated disclosure should govern the contract. Try it with your own numbers in the [APR Calculator](/apr-calculator) — the result updates as you type, so you can test a few scenarios in seconds.

### Does APR include compounding?

The APR shown here is a nominal annual rate derived from the monthly borrowing cost. A separate effective annual rate is included to show annual compounding. Try it with your own numbers in the [APR Calculator](/apr-calculator) — the result updates as you type, so you can test a few scenarios in seconds.

### What formula does the APR Calculator use?

Payment = P·r ÷ (1 − (1+r)⁻ⁿ). APR is found by solving net proceeds = payment × (1 − (1+a)⁻ⁿ) ÷ a for monthly APR rate a, then multiplying a by 12 × 100. You can see it in action in the [APR Calculator](/apr-calculator) — enter your own values and the result updates as you type.
